articles.title: GPs are now ‘prescribing’ time in nature. Is it likely to improve your health?
articles.author: Lauren Ball, Professor of Community Health and Wellbeing, The University of Queensland
articles.summary: The advice might be to spend 20 minutes a day noticing the natural world – whether that’s walking through a park, listening to birds or wildlife gardening.
articles.contentHtml:
Imagine visiting your GP for your physical or mental health and leaving with a prescription to spend more time outdoors.

This is becoming a reality in Australia, with the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners recently endorsing resources to help doctors recommend spending time in nature.

The advice includes spending 20 minutes a day noticing the natural world – whether that’s walking through a park, listening to birds or wildlife gardening.

Spending time in nature has recognised health benefits. But does a doctor’s recommendation actually mean people are more likely to experience those benefits?

What do we know about nature and health?

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have long recognised the importance of connection to Country for health and wellbeing. This connection encompasses relationships with land, waters, culture, community and identity.

Over recent decades, researchers have investigated whether spending time in nature can benefit our physical and mental health. But the strength of evidence varies depending on the activity and health outcome being measured.

A recent review assessed the evidence for nature prescribing on mental health. The reviewers examined 47 trials with almost 3,800 participants, including nature walks, outdoor exercise and gardening. Of these, 17 found significant improvements in mental health compared with control groups, particularly for depression, anxiety and stress.

A further 15 studies found some benefits, although these were less consistent. The researchers concluded that nature-based activities show promise for improving mental health, but more rigorous studies are needed to understand their longer-term benefits.

There may also be benefits for physical health. A review of 22 studies examining forest-based activities found improvements in blood pressure, heart rate variability and cortisol, a hormone associated with stress.

However, findings for blood glucose, or blood sugar, were less consistent.

So how much time should we spend outdoors?

A recommendation of two hours per week comes largely from a study involving almost 20,000 adults in England.

People who spent at least two hours in nature each week were more likely to report good health and wellbeing than those who spent no time in nature.

However, this was an observational study. It found an association between nature exposure and health, rather than demonstrating that two hours of nature causes better health.

The amount of time needed to experience benefits may vary between people, and we don’t yet know whether there is an ideal amount of time for everyone.

Does prescribing nature actually work?

This is where things become more complicated.

Nature prescribing is a form of social prescribing. This is a way health professionals encourage patients to participate in activities that support their health and wellbeing.

A nature prescription might involve recommending regular park walks, community gardening or participation in a local conservation group.

But there’s an important difference between knowing that spending time in nature can benefit health and knowing whether a GP’s recommendation helps people experience those benefits.

Research into nature prescribing is growing, with programs such as Canada’s PaRx and Park Rx America in the United States providing examples of how health professionals can encourage patients to spend time outdoors.

England’s green social prescribing multi-site trial enabled more than 8,000 participants to access nature-based activities. Community link workers also supported referred patients to engage with local activities. Participants reported significant improvements in their mental health.

A review of 92 studies also found nature prescribing delivered by health or social professionals improved participants’ blood pressure and mental health, and increased the number of steps they took each day.

The evidence for nature prescribing remains limited by differences in how programs are delivered, how referrals are provided, and how outcomes are measured.

It’s difficult to know whether improvements come from spending time in nature, increased physical activity, social connection, or the additional encouragement provided by a health professional.

There are also challenges for GPs. Not all doctors are familiar with the evidence for nature prescribing or know which local activities and services are available to their patients.

Without this knowledge, it can be difficult to turn a recommendation to spend more time outdoors into practical advice that patients can follow.

What would make nature prescribing successful?

Recommending time outdoors might sound straightforward. But following that advice isn’t equally easy for everyone.

Some people have access to safe and welcoming local parks. But someone working long hours, managing a disability or living in an area with limited quality green space may face greater challenges.

This means nature prescribing needs to consider people’s circumstances, preferences and access to suitable outdoor environments.

Research also suggests successful clinician-led referrals require:

  • local knowledge of nature-based activities
  • confidence that recommended activities are safe and accessible for their patients
  • alignment with patients’ interests.

It may also require more than a conversation during a GP appointment.

Connecting patients with local walking groups, community gardens or other structured activities such as conservation volunteering could help turn a recommendation into something practical.

Our research is currently exploring how nature prescribing might work in everyday health care.

So should we follow a nature prescription?

Spending time in nature is generally accessible and can offer benefits for physical, mental and social wellbeing.

The the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners’ endorsement of nature prescribing is an opportunity for GPs to discuss these benefits with patients.

But we still need stronger evidence about whether nature prescribing itself improves health outcomes, which patients benefit most and how to make it work in practice.

For now, spending time outdoors is something many people can try, with or without a prescription. The challenge is ensuring everyone has opportunities to enjoy the benefits.

Lauren Ball receives funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council, Health and Wellbeing Queensland, Heart Foundation, Gallipoli Medical Research and Mater Health, Springfield City Group. She is a director of Dietitians Australia, a director of the Darling Downs and West Moreton Primary Health Network and an associate member of the Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences.

Victoria is a volunteer Walk Organiser and Local Coordinator with the Heart Foundation Walking Program (registered charity), and a volunteer member of the nature-based health committee with Outdoors Queensland (not-for profit organisation).

articles.title: Some antidepressants may work better than others long term – new study
articles.author: Jack Janetzki, Lecturer in Pharmacy and Pharmacology, Adelaide University
articles.summary: The research review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. Here’s what you need to know.
articles.contentHtml:
A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Why do people take antidepressants long term?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

What did the researchers find?

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomised controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

How reliable are the findings?

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term”. The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

What this research can’t tell us

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

What’s the best fit for you?

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: What science says about perimenopause, menopause and mood swings — minus the hype
articles.author: Jennifer L. Gordon, Professor, Psychology, University of Regina
articles.summary: The link between between this transition and mental health is real but more complicated than the ‘meno-boom’ suggests.
articles.contentHtml:
After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere — in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the “meno-boom,” and booms attract business.

The Canadian menopause wellness market — meaning the products, treatments and services designed and sold to help women manage symptoms before, during and after menopause — is projected to reach a revenue of US$784.9 million by 2030.

But alongside the marketing are sensational claims and outright misinformation, including about how the menopausal transition affects mental health. That’s exactly what my research team has been studying for more than a decade.

And as a woman now navigating perimenopause myself, I have a personal appreciation for why these conversations matter. I’m far from being in a minority: the Canadian Institutes of Health Research estimates that about 10 million people in Canada are currently navigating some stage of perimenopause, menopause or post-menopause transition.

So let’s cut through the noise. Here’s what the evidence actually says about menopause and mental health.

Before you know you’re in perimenopause

The increased risk of depressive mood arises early in what researchers call the early menopause transition. This stage is marked by menstrual cycles that are consistently seven days shorter or longer relative to a woman’s usual cycle.

Someone whose cycle used to average 30 days, for example, might start having 23- or 37-day cycles.

So unless you’re tracking your cycle very closely, it can be easy to miss any connection between mid-life mood changes and perimenopause. It also doesn’t help that depressive symptoms have been shown to fluctuate considerably in perimenopause, making it a moving target.

Not just about depression and mood swings

Though a lot of research on the menopause transition has focused on depressed mood, there’s growing recognition that other psychological symptoms can show up too.

For example, a recent study by our team, following perimenopausal women for three months, found that more than half struggled with moderate-to-severe anger and irritability. Weekly changes in sleep quality, hot flash severity, as well as hormones, predicted weekly changes in anger.

Estrogen fluctuation in perimenopause has also been associated with greater sensitivity to interpersonal rejection, highlighting that psychological changes in the menopause transition can involve more than just feeling down.

This fits with anecdotes from women that say they just “don’t feel like themselves.”

Read more: Perimenopause usually begins in your 40s. How do you know if it has started?

Hot flashes don’t explain everything

Hot flashes are no fun, and they are extremely common in mid-life, with 60 to 80 per cent of women experiencing them in the years leading up to and following their last menstrual period. But as much as hot flashes may negatively impact quality of life, they don’t fully account for the increase in low mood that we see in perimenopause.

For one thing, the timing doesn’t line up. Across the population, mood symptoms begin to increase well before hot flashes emerge. And by the time hot flashes reach their peak severity, depressive symptoms are already declining.

At an individual level, this translates to many women experiencing depressive mood in the absence of hot flashes and many others experiencing hot flashes in the absence of mood changes.

Hormone therapy isn’t a cure-all

Menopausal hormone therapy is highly effective in treating hot flashes and night sweats. Vaginal estrogen cream is also a safe and effective treatment for vaginal dryness and sexual difficulties at any age.

The benefits for cognitive difficulties (memory and thinking), sleep and low mood are less well-established.

Multiple rigorous trials have confirmed that menopausal hormone therapy doesn’t prevent cognitive decline. And though it has been shown to improve sleep difficulties in women experiencing night sweats, evidence for its benefits in women without these symptoms is less conclusive.

As for mood, the overall benefits of menopausal hormone therapy have been found to be quite modest, although some women may benefit more than others. Cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin-based antidepressants remain the first-line treatments for depressive symptoms, including during perimenopause.

Future research may help us better pinpoint who stands to benefit most from hormone therapy. In the meantime, it’s worth keeping both its proven benefits and the limits of the current evidence in view.

Not everyone struggles with the transition

The increased attention paid to menopause and perimenopause is long overdue, and it stands to greatly improve mid-life care. Women should not have to suffer in silence or go untreated. But we should be mindful about how we discuss it.

Women have long been dismissed as “hormonal” — meaning less logical, rational and level-headed than men. Careless narratives or conversations about menopause risk reinforcing that stereotype.

Our research consistently finds enormous individual differences in how sensitive women are to the hormonal changes occurring in the menopause transition. For some, rapid shifts in hormone levels can trigger a host of negative mood symptoms. For others, the effects are negligible.

Women experiencing difficult symptoms deserve recognition and effective treatment. But mid-life can also bring greater confidence, autonomy and opportunities for personal and professional growth. For some, menopause also means welcome freedom from menstruation and concerns about pregnancy.

The “meno-boom” has brought perimenopause out of the shadows, and that’s worth celebrating. But attention isn’t the same as understanding. The research reveals that this period is more complicated (and more individual) than pop culture and business marketing can capture.

Taking women’s mid-life mental health seriously means resisting easy answers.

Jennifer L. Gordon receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR).

articles.title: Does time on social media make teens anxious and depressed? The evidence is not so clear
articles.author: John Gleeson, Professor and Director Healthy Brain and Mind Research Centre, Australian Catholic University
articles.summary: The social media ban for under-16s may stem from concern about a very real mental health crisis. But is it missing the point?
articles.contentHtml:
Parents are understandably worried about the impact of social media on the mental health of their children.

In the last two decades, mental health disorders have significantly increased among 16-to-24-year-old Australians, affecting 39% in 2022, up from 26% in 2007. Over the same period, smartphones have given young people continuous access to social media.

But questions remain about whether there is a causal link: does spending time on social media harm young people’s mental health?

This can be difficult to study directly. In our new research, we analysed the findings of 37 studies examining the relationship between social media use and anxiety and depression symptoms in young people aged 10–24. We were surprised to find only a very weak link between the time they spent on social media and their levels of anxiety and depression.

This suggests simply restricting young people’s access to social media – the focus of recent policies – may be missing the broader picture when it comes to addressing anxiety and depression.

The tide has turned against social media

When the social media restrictions for under-16s came into effect in December 2025, Australia placed itself at the forefront of global efforts to protect young people from social media via regulation.

Other countries, including the United Kingdom and Spain, are poised to follow suit or are watching Australia closely.

We hope that social media restrictions will indeed improve the wellbeing of young people. However, our unexpected research findings mean we’re not optimistic – and suggest the solution will be far more complex.

What we looked at

We collated evidence from 37 longitudinal and experimental studies that in total tracked nearly 80,000 young people’s social media use and their symptoms of depression and anxiety over time. The studies were conducted across 15 mainly high-income countries – including Australia – using highly representative samples of the wider population of young people.

Interestingly, we found only one experimental study (meaning researchers intervene to control variables to isolate a particular effect). Its findings suggested restricting social media might be beneficial if young people were already severely depressed.

The other 36 were all observational studies (meaning researchers don’t intervene, but record what they observe to see if there are patterns or relationships).

We pooled information about linear relationships to see if, as time using social media increased, depression and anxiety symptoms became more severe.

What we found

We were surprised to find only a very weak association. Overall social media use accounted for less than 1% of how much anxiety and depression symptoms varied in severity.

This effect was not stronger in younger compared to older adolescents. Nor was the effect stronger in more recent studies, when social media platforms have increasingly adopted features to maximise engagement such as algorithmic feeds, infinite scrolling and push notifications.

Read more: Can’t stop endlessly scrolling? Tips to help you take back control

In our synthesis we focused on anxiety and depressive symptoms. Of course, it’s possible that time on social media platforms has stronger links to other mental health symptoms, such as body image problems, or worse outcomes at school.

Just measuring the time someone spends on social media also doesn’t capture whether they’re exposed to harmful content, such as cyberbullying.

What the one direct experiment found

In the single experimental study we found, researchers assigned 182 young people to different groups, in which they either continued to use social media as normal, or limited their use.

Participants who had their social media use capped at one hour a day, and who were already highly depressed, reported a decrease in symptoms. Highly depressed participants in the control group did not.

This suggests restrictions could help young people who are already suffering from high levels of depressive symptoms.

What does all this mean?

Despite the findings of the one experimental study, the takeaway from our synthesis of the strongest available evidence is that social media restrictions alone may not successfully address the mental health crisis.

Researchers and policymakers also need to explore other potential causes and solutions. Other factors under active investigation include the changing academic pressures young people face, as well as inequality, job insecurity, housing stress, climate change and substance use.

Of course, increases in mental health problems rarely boil down to one cause, but are likely due to a complex interaction of such factors.

There is also growing interest among researchers in young people’s increasing awareness and evolving concepts of mental health and mental illness. A young person today may seek a diagnosis for levels of distress that, in previous decades, might have gone undetected. This potentially affects how young people self-report mental health, as well as the treatment they receive.

Read more: Mentally, are young people really worse off? Or are they better at admitting they’re struggling?

Australia’s social media restrictions for under-16 year olds are an important opportunity to test the impact on young people’s mental health. However, we cannot assume they will stem the tide of growing mental health problems.

In the meantime, understanding and responding to the underlying causes of the mental health crisis remains a critical priority.

If this article has raised issues for you, or if you’re concerned about someone you know, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800.

We would like to acknowledge the contribution of former Honours student William Peachey in preparing this article.

John Gleeson has received research grant funding from the Australian Research Council, National Health and Medical Research Council, and Wellcome Trust.

articles.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
articles.author: Jason Walker, Associate Professor of Psychology, Health and Wellness, Adler University
articles.summary: The rates are similar to high-stress workplaces like emergency services.
articles.contentHtml:
Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades, according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo.

Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.

Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently.

Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.

More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations.

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services, according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice.

Why it matters

Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions.

Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.

Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.

How we did our work

We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K.

Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.

The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines.

Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.

What still isn’t known

Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.

Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities.

Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture.

Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts.

Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.

The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

Jason Walker does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
articles.author: Sarah Chellappa, Associate Professor, Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, University of Southampton
articles.summary: Research shows that disrupted body clocks can affect mood. A circadian rhythms researcher explains how sleep, light and meal timing influence mental health.
articles.contentHtml:
Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role.

Our circadian rhythms are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion.

Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut.

When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges.

Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning.

These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing.

In a 2024 laboratory study, my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities.

We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour.

We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines.

Circadian disruption has also been linked to depression and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood.

The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another.

What happens when our clocks fall out of sync

Night shift workers may need to stay awake when their bodies are preparing for sleep and rest when their internal clocks promote alertness.

This mismatch is known as circadian misalignment.

In a 2020 study, we investigated how this misalignment affected mood in two controlled laboratory experiments involving people with and without shift-work experience.

Participants followed schedules designed to simulate day and night shifts while all other behavioural and environmental factors were controlled for, including light exposure, physical activity, food intake and opportunities for sleep.

We found that mood and wellbeing reduced when participants’ sleeping and waking schedules were misaligned with their internal body clock. The effects were observed in non-shift workers as well as shift workers.

These findings suggest circadian misalignment can influence mood, although larger studies are needed to establish the long-term consequences.

Outside the laboratory, many people experience a mismatch known as social jetlag. This occurs when people’s sleep and waking times differ substantially between working days and days off.

Artificial light can also affect our internal clocks. Bright light in the evening, including light from electronic screens, can suppress melatonin and delay our sleep time.

My research on light sensitivity has highlighted differences between individuals. Some people’s circadian rhythms are much more sensitive to evening light than others, meaning the same exposure may have different effects.

Could changing meal times help?

Light is the strongest environmental signal for the master clock, but eating also influences the timing of biological processes in other organs.

In a 2022 study, my colleagues and I investigated whether changing meal times could reduce the effects of simulated night work on mood.

Nineteen healthy volunteers followed carefully controlled schedules designed to mimic night shifts. One group ate during both the day and night, while the other ate only during the daytime.

Among participants who ate during both periods, ratings of depression-like mood increased by 26.2% and anxiety-like mood by 16.1% compared with their baseline measurements.

We did not observe significant increases in either measure among those who ate only during the daytime.

These findings suggest that the timing of meals may influence how circadian disruption affects mood. However, the study involved a small group of healthy volunteers under laboratory conditions. Further research involving shift workers is needed to establish whether eating only during the daytime can help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression.

How to support your body clock

Although we may not control our working hours or sleep schedules, some daily habits may help keep our internal clocks aligned.

  1. Get morning daylight. Light is the most powerful environmental signal for the master clock. Spending time outdoors after waking can support alertness and help regulate the timing of sleep later. The amount of light needed varies between people.

Read more: Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains

  1. Reduce bright light before bed. Dimming household lights and limiting screen use in the evening/night-time may help the body prepare for sleep. The NHS recommends avoiding electronic screens for at least an hour before bedtime.

  2. Keep a regular sleep-wake schedule. Going to bed and waking up at reasonably consistent times can help reinforce circadian rhythms. A systematic review associated regular sleep patterns with better health outcomes, including diabetes, heart diseases and depression.

  3. Consider food and exercise timing. Consistent and earlier food times may help support the body’s daily rhythms for physical health, although research is needed to establish the best eating schedules for mental health. Regular physical activity can also benefit sleep. A review of studies found that evening exercise generally did not interfere with sleep, although vigorous exercise ending very close to bedtime sometimes did.

Protecting sleep and mental health

Research suggests that the timing of sleep and daily activities can influence mood, although more evidence is needed to establish whether changing these routines can help prevent or treat mental health conditions.

Maintaining consistent routines and getting enough sleep may support emotional wellbeing, but these habits cannot replace appropriate treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep or mood problems should seek medical advice. Understanding how our internal clocks influence mood may eventually offer new ways to support mental health.
